content: The evaluation of a country’s claim to have interrupted the transmission of the onchocercal parasite involves a thorough review of the submitted dossier, which includes a field visit to the country. Based on this assessment, recommendations are made to the World Health Organization (WHO) to either support or reject the national claim of transmission interruption. The status of elimination can only be granted to a country by the WHO Director-General after all identified transmission foci under long-term ivermectin treatment have been verified as free of transmission. Additionally, sufficient evidence must demonstrate that all potential areas of transmission have been identified, ensuring that the transmission of Onchocerca volvulus no longer occurs in the country. This determination is based on the findings of an international verification team. The elimination of O. volvulus transmission cannot be confirmed until a sufficient number of years of ivermectin treatment and post-treatment surveillance have been completed. In cases where transmission persists in neighboring countries, WHO may withhold acknowledgment of elimination until surrounding areas have also interrupted transmission. If elimination is documented through appropriate testing of black flies and corroborated by serological evaluation of children under 10 years of age, the national program must establish a post-elimination surveillance system. This system is designed to detect any potential resurgence or reintroduction of parasite transmission in previously endemic, non-endemic, or high-risk areas where imported cases might occur. Post-elimination surveillance often relies on entomological assessments, such as demonstrating the absence of infective-stage larvae of O. volvulus in vector populations using O-150 PCR with species-specific DNA probes. Future revisions of these guidelines are anticipated to incorporate new discoveries, such as improved diagnostic assays or novel interventions, which will be tested and validated under field conditions. These innovations, if deemed suitable, will be included in updated guidelines for consideration by 2020. Additionally, further clarification on the co-endemicity of onchocerciasis and lymphatic filariasis is expected as more programs encounter this situation and draw specific lessons. The metrics for controlling onchocerciasis have been extensively supported by field and modeling-based research. Widely used models, such as ONCHOSIM, SIMON, and the refined EUSIMON model for the Americas, have addressed various questions related to elimination, including the persistence of onchocerciasis under different ecological conditions and the feasibility of elimination through vector control and mass drug administration (MDA). Despite advancements in understanding onchocerciasis control and elimination, current and future strategies face challenges, such as the impact of macrofilaricides on long-term ivermectin distribution and the potential to shorten the duration of annual, biannual, or quarterly MDA until elimination is achieved. The guidelines for stopping MDA and verifying the elimination of human onchocerciasis will be launched at a suitable event to maximize visibility. The guidelines will also be made available electronically on the WHO website in a downloadable format.
